content: Epinephrine is a medication used to treat wheezing and shortness of breath, which are common symptoms of asthma. By controlling these symptoms, it can help reduce time lost from work or school. Epinephrine belongs to a class of drugs called bronchodilators, which work by relaxing the muscles around the airways, allowing them to open and making breathing easier. To use this medication, carefully read the patient information leaflet for instructions on proper use and cleaning of the mouthpiece. Shake the canister well before each inhalation. Follow all directions on the product packaging, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use the medication exactly as directed. Inhale it through the mouth as needed. Remove the cap from the mouthpiece, place it near your mouth, and exhale. Insert the mouthpiece fully into your mouth, press the inhaler, and breathe in deeply. Hold your breath for as long as comfortable to allow the drug to be absorbed. If more than one inhalation is required, wait at least one full minute between inhalations. Do not use the medication again for at least four hours. Rinse your mouth after use to prevent dryness and throat irritation. Clean the mouthpiece daily as directed. Keep track of the number of inhalations used from each canister, and discard the canister once the marked number of inhalations has been used. Common side effects of epinephrine include headache, nausea, vomiting, nervousness, dizziness, shaking (tremor), trouble sleeping, stomach upset, sweating, dry mouth, bad taste, cough, or sore throat. If your doctor has prescribed this medication, they have determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, it can cause severe and sudden worsening of breathing problems or asthma (paradoxical bronchospasm). Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. If you experience any severe symptoms, such as passing out or difficulty breathing, seek emergency medical attention immediately. Before using epinephrine, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, similar bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol, levalbuterol, salmeterol), sympathomimetic drugs (e.g., pseudoephedrine), or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that can cause allergic reactions or other problems. Epinephrine may cause dizziness, and alcohol or marijuana can worsen this effect. Avoid driving, using machinery, or performing tasks requiring alertness until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly needed. It is unknown if this drug passes into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Avoid taking monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors (e.g., isocarboxazid, phenelzine, tranylcypromine) or tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline, nortriptyline) within two weeks before, during, or after treatment with this medication. Caffeine can increase the side effects of epinephrine. In case of overdose, if someone has serious symptoms such as passing out or trouble breathing, call emergency services immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. In the U.S., call 1-800-222-1222, and in Canada, call 1-844-764-7669. Store epinephrine at room temperature, away from direct sunlight. Do not puncture the canister or expose it to high heat or open flames. Avoid storing it in the bathroom. Properly discard the product when it is expired or no longer needed. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Epinephrine is the first-line medication of choice for treating anaphylaxis and should be used promptly in emergencies. It is also used to manage wheezing and shortness of breath associated with asthma. Always seek immediate medical or hospital care after using this medication.
